questions.q: The length of a metal wire is found to be $L_1$ and $L_2$ when the tension of $T_1$ and $T_2$ are applied to it respectively. The natural length of the wire is
questions.solution:
As $Y=$ Young's modulus of material
$=\frac{F / A}{\Delta L / L_0}\Rightarrow \quad \Delta L=\frac{L_0 F}{Y A} \Rightarrow L-L_0=\frac{L_0 F}{Y A}\Rightarrow \quad L=L_0+\frac{L_0 F}{Y A}$
Here, $\quad L_1=L_0+\frac{L_0 T_1}{Y A}\ldots$ (i)
and $\quad L_2=L_0+\frac{L_0 T_2}{Y A}\ldots$ (ii)
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we have
$\left(L_1-L_0\right) T_2=\frac{L_0 T_1 T_2}{Y A} \text{ and }\left(L_2-L_0\right) T_1=\frac{L_0 T_1 T_2}{Y A}$
So, equating we have
$\Rightarrow \quad\left(L_1-L_0\right) T_2=\left(L_2-L_0\right) T_1\Rightarrow \quad L_1 T_2-L_2 T_1=L_0\left(T_2-T_1\right)\Rightarrow \quad L_0=\frac{L_1 T_2-L_2 T_1}{T_2-T_1}$

Bulk modulus is given by

So, fractional compression (in $\%$ ) is

questions.solution:
Given, ratio of length of copper wire and
aluminium wire, $l_1: l_2=5: 2$
and diameter ratio of the wire $=d_1: d_2=4: 3\therefore \quad r_1: r_2=2: \frac{3}{2}$
If $\Delta l_1$ and $\Delta l_2$ are increase in the length of copper and aluminium wire, respectively then for copper wire,
$\Delta l_1=\frac{F_1 l_1}{A_1 y_1}$
For aluminium wire,
$\Delta l_2=\frac{F_2 l_2}{A_2 y_2}$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$\frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta l_2}=\frac{l_1}{l_2} \cdot \frac{A_2}{A_1} \cdot \frac{y_2}{y_1} \cdot \frac{F_1}{F_2} \quad\left[\because \frac{y_2}{y_1}=\frac{y_{\mathrm{Al}}}{y_{\mathrm{Cu}}}=\frac{0.7}{1.1}\right]=\frac{5}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi r_2^2}{\pi r_1^2} \cdot \frac{0.7 \times 10^{11}}{1.1 \times 10^{11}} \cdot \frac{4}{5} \quad\left[\because\right.$ Given, $\left.\frac{F_1}{F_2}=\frac{4}{5}\right]=\frac{5}{2} \cdot \frac{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2}{(2)^2} \times \frac{7}{11} \times \frac{4}{5}=\frac{63}{88}$
Hence, the ratio of increase in length of the copper and aluminium wire will be $\frac{63}{88}$.

questions.q: A uniform rod of length $L$ is rotated in a horizontal plane about a vertical axis through one of its ends. The angular speed of rotation is $\omega$. Find increase in length of the rod, if $\rho$ and $Y$ are the density and Young's modulus of the rod respectively,
questions.solution:
Given,
length of uniform $\operatorname{rod}=L$
angular speed $=\omega$
and density of rod $=\rho$
When rod is rotated in a horizontal plane, centrifugal force is responsible for increasing the length of rod, which is also equal to stress.
If $d l$ be the change in length of small element $d x$ due to rotation, by application of force $d F$. Young's modulus, $\begin{aligned}& Y=\frac{\text{ stress }}{\text{ strain }}=\frac{d F / A}{d l / x}\\
\Rightarrow \quad & d l=\frac{d F \cdot x}{A Y}\\
\Rightarrow \quad & d F=\frac{A Y d l}{x}
\end{aligned}$ Where, $d F=$ centrifugal force due to mass of the element of length, $d x$. $\begin{aligned} d F & =d m \cdot x \omega^2 \\
d F & =\frac{m}{L} \cdot x d x \omega^2 \\
& \quad \ldots \text{ (ii) }\\
& {\left[\because \text{ Change$ in $mass } d m=\frac{m}{L} d x\right] }
\end{aligned} From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get \begin{aligned}\frac{A Y d l}{x}& =\frac{m}{L} \cdot x d x \omega^2 \\
\Rightarrow \quad d l & =\frac{m x^2 \omega^2}{L A Y} \cdot d x
\end{aligned} \Rightarrow Total change in length, \begin{aligned} l & =\int d l=\int_0^L \frac{m x^2 \omega^2}{L A Y} d x \\
& =\frac{m \omega^2 L^2}{3 A Y}=\frac{m}{A L} \cdot \frac{\omega^2 L^3}{3 Y}=\frac{\rho \omega^2 L^3}{3 Y}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Assertion (a) : Ductile metals are used to prepare thin wires.Reason (R): In the stress-strain curve of ductile metals, the length between the points representing elastic limit and breaking point is very small.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution: Assertion (A) is true. Ductile metals are materials that can be stretched or drawn into thin wires without breaking. This property, known as ductility, is essential for manufacturing wires for applications like electrical wiring and cables. Gold, silver, and copper are examples of highly ductile metals. Reason (R) is false. The stress-strain curve for a ductile material has a long plastic deformation region between the elastic limit and the breaking point. This is precisely what defines a ductile material-it can undergo significant permanent deformation (plastic deformation) before it fractures. In contrast, a brittle material has a very small or non-existent plastic region, breaking soon after its elastic limit is reached. The correct option is (3) (A) is true but (R) is false.

questions.q: Water in a river $20 \mathrm{ m}$ deep is flowing at a speed of $10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$. The shearing stress between the horizontal layers of water in the river in $\mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$ is (Coefficient of viscosity of water $=10^{-3} \mathrm{ \ SI}$ units)
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \text{ Shearing stress } & =\eta\left(\frac{d v}{d x}\right) \\ & =10^{-3}\left(\frac{10}{20}\right) \\ & =0.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The Poisson's ratio of a material is 0.4. If a force is applied to a wire of this material, there is a decrease of cross-sectional area by $2 \%$. The percentage increase in its length is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text{ Poission's ratio } \sigma=\frac{\Delta R / R}{\Delta l / l} \\ & \frac{\Delta l}{l}=\frac{\Delta R}{R} \times \frac{1}{\sigma} \\ & =\frac{\Delta R}{R} \times \frac{1}{0.4} \\ & \therefore \text{ Increase$ in $length }=\left(\frac{\Delta R}{R} \times \frac{1}{0.4}\right) \times 100 \\ & =\frac{2}{2} \times \frac{1}{0.4}=2.5 \% \\ & \end{aligned}$
